title: France sets out 10-year nuclear fusion roadmap
excerpt: France unveils 10-year nuclear fusion roadmap to strengthen research, develop specialist skills and support a European pilot plant by 2035.
content:
France has unveiled a ten-year nuclear fusion roadmap designed to coordinate national research, strengthen scientific expertise and accelerate the development of fusion energy.

Published by the Ministry of Research, the strategy sets out priorities for investment, infrastructure and workforce development through to 2035, and centres on three major research facilities: the international ITER project, the CEA’s WEST tokamak, and the Laser Mégajoule inertial confinement facility.

Together, these installations will underpin France’s efforts to advance fusion research and strengthen its contribution to the technology’s development.

Alongside scientific and technological progress, the strategy aims to double the number of students pursuing relevant disciplines, including plasma physics, nuclear engineering and cryogenic technologies.

The ambition reflects the importance of developing a skilled workforce capable of supporting the next stages of fusion research.

Speaking on the roadmap, French Minister for Higher Education, Research and Space Philippe Baptiste commented: “We all know the importance of working on fusion, on the future of energy, to have an energy source that is available and also carbon-free.

“Not only are we strongly supporting ITER, which is a key asset, but we also want to develop national equipment that can also help provide some additional technologies that can be crucial for successful development.”

What is fusion energy?

Nuclear fusion is the process through which two light atomic nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy in the process. It is the same fundamental reaction that powers the Sun and other stars.

Scientists are investigating how to reproduce this process on Earth as a potential source of low-carbon energy. However, achieving and sustaining the conditions required for fusion remains a significant scientific and engineering challenge.

Two phases towards fusion energy

The roadmap divides its objectives into short- and medium-term priorities, with the first phase covering 2026 to 2030.

During this period, France intends to strengthen the scientific foundations of fusion research, expand its experimental capabilities and consolidate existing technical expertise. Securing the funding needed to support these activities is also central to the strategy.

Looking further ahead, the government wants the necessary technologies to be available by 2035 to support the development of a European pilot fusion plant.

The roadmap therefore places considerable emphasis on preparing the research infrastructure, technical capabilities and specialist workforce needed to move towards this longer-term objective.

ITER and WEST central to France’s strategy

The nuclear fusion roadmap was formally presented during a visit by Minister Baptiste to the CEA research centre, following a tour of the nearby ITER construction site alongside ITER Director-General Pietro Barabaschi.

The visit highlighted the importance of the facilities underpinning France’s fusion programme, particularly ITER and the WEST tokamak, which provide important infrastructure for advancing research.

By combining investment in major experimental facilities with efforts to expand scientific expertise and education, France’s nuclear fusion roadmap establishes a framework for progressing towards the technologies required for a European pilot plant by 2035.
